The Galilean moons. From left to right, in order of increasing distance from Jupiter: [Io](/wiki/Io_(moon) "Io (moon)"); [Europa](/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)"); [Ganymede](/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)"); [Callisto](/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)").

The physical and orbital characteristics of the moons vary widely. The four Galileans are all over 3,100 kilometres (1,900 mi) in diameter;[[4]](#cite_note-4) the largest Galilean, [Ganymede](/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)"), is the ninth [largest object](/wiki/List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size "List of Solar System objects by size") in the [Solar System](/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System"), after the Sun and seven of the [planets](/wiki/Planet "Planet"), Ganymede being larger than [Mercury](/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)").[[5]](#cite_note-5) All other Jovian moons are less than 250 kilometres (160 mi) in diameter, with most barely exceeding 5 kilometres (3.1 mi).[[note 1]](#cite_note-6) Their [orbital shapes](/wiki/Orbit "Orbit") range from nearly perfectly circular to highly [eccentric](/wiki/Orbital_eccentricity "Orbital eccentricity") and [inclined](/wiki/Inclination "Inclination"), and many revolve in the direction opposite to Jupiter's rotation ([retrograde motion](/wiki/Retrograde_motion "Retrograde motion")).[[6]](#cite_note-jpllist-7)
